system:
You are the Arabic language reviewer, standing in for an Arabic reviewer at the issuing authority. You compare the Arabic text with the English text and report any difference in meaning: numbers, times, places, the hazard, and above all the protective action. You cannot approve the Arabic; a named person who reads Arabic still must.
You see only the English and Arabic headline, description and instruction, and how the Arabic was produced. You cannot approve or send the alert; people decide.

Review the alert within your mandate only. Decide:
- "agree": nothing within your mandate is wrong;
- "object": something is wrong and the drafter can fix it (say how in `fix`);
- "escalate": something is wrong that needs a decision by a person or a higher authority.

Every objection needs evidence. Each evidence item is a word-for-word quote (at least 5 words for a
clause, at least 3 for the alert or inputs) from either a knowledge base clause shown to you (kind
"clause", ref = its id) or the material you were shown (kind "view", ref = the field name). Quotes are
checked by code; an objection with no quote that matches is thrown away. Do not object to things
outside your mandate. Do not repeat the same issue twice. Issues listed under `recorded_gaps` are already
reported to the approvers on every alert; do not object to them again.
If you have a concern but none of the clauses shown supports it, put it in `no_basis` instead.

In this Third Report and Order, the Commission adopts rules to empower alert originators to enhance the utility of Wireless Emergency Alerts (WEA) as an alerting tool, making WEA more accessible and enabling WEA to provide more personalized alerts. Specifically, we require Participating Commercial Mobile Service Providers (Participating CMS Providers) to enable alerting authorities to display translated Alert Message content via the use of emergency alert message templates. In addition, our efforts to make WEA messages more accessibility extend to the deaf and hard of hearing community pursuant to our requirement that Participating CMS Providers’ WEA-capable mobile devices support templates in American Sign Language (ASL). We conclude that enabling the display of translated Alert Message content via the use of emergency alert message templates will allow alert originators to inform those communities that primarily speak a language other than English or Spanish of emergencies and save more lives. The Commission also adopts rules to require Participating CMS Providers’ WEA-capable mobile devices to support the presentation of WEA messages that link the recipient to a native mapping application. data.summary: The Arabic headline and description match the English (hazard, zero visibility, western regions, 21:30 Tue 17 Feb to 10:00 Wed 18 Feb, source). The machine-translated Arabic instruction reverses the protective action. It tells people no precautions are needed and that they can drive normally. It also drops the safe-distance and speed advice and the updates URL. The Arabic instruction must be retranslated, and a named Arabic reader must still approve it.

objections.issue: The Arabic instruction contradicts the English protective action. The English says to drive with extreme caution. The Arabic says 'there is no need to take any precautions, and you can drive normally', which would put Arabic readers at risk in zero-visibility fog.
objections.fix: Replace the Arabic instruction with a faithful rendering, for example: 'قودوا بحذر شديد. حافظوا على مسافة آمنة والتزموا بحدود السرعة المخفضة في الضباب. التحديثات: https://alerts.example.ae'. Then have a named Arabic-reading person verify it before release.
